name: VLF/LF fixed and maritime mobile
notes: The standard-time transmitters live here: WWVB and MSF on 60 kHz, DCF77 on 77.5 kHz. Most receivers need direct sampling or an upconverter to reach it.

name: DCF77 — time signal
notes: 77.5 kHz from Mainflingen: the amplitude-keyed code every German radio clock listens to, one bit a second.

name: 2200 m amateur
notes: 1 W EIRP in most administrations: CW, WSPR and other very slow modes.

name: Long-wave broadcast
notes: A Region 1 speciality. 9 kHz raster; several transmitters also carry a time code, as 162 kHz did for France.

name: Maritime radio beacons and DGPS
notes: Differential GPS corrections, MSK at 100–200 bit/s.

name: Aeronautical non-directional beacons
notes: A keyed carrier repeating a two- or three-letter Morse ident.

name: 630 m amateur
notes: 5 W EIRP in most administrations: CW, WSPR and FT8.

name: NAVTEX — 490 kHz
notes: National-language navigational warnings. SITOR-B, 100 baud FSK with a 170 Hz shift.

name: Maritime mobile (MF)
notes: 500 kHz was the international distress and calling frequency until 1999.

name: NAVTEX — 518 kHz
notes: The international NAVTEX service, always in English. SITOR-B, 100 baud FSK.

name: Medium-wave broadcast (Region 2)
notes: 10 kHz raster, and the band runs 100 kHz higher than elsewhere.

name: Medium-wave broadcast
notes: 9 kHz raster in Regions 1 and 3. Groundwave by day, skywave after dark.

name: 160 m amateur
notes: Lower sideband by convention. A night band: daytime absorption kills it.

name: 160 m amateur (Region 1)
notes: Region 1 starts at 1810 kHz, not 1800.

name: Maritime mobile (2 MHz)
notes: 2182 kHz is the MF distress and calling frequency.

name: HF aeronautical mobile (route)
notes: Upper sideband. Long-haul oceanic and polar air traffic control.

name: 80 m amateur (Region 1)
notes: 300 kHz here against 500 kHz in Region 2; 3.8–3.9 MHz is broadcast.

name: HF fixed, mobile and amateur (80 m)
notes: How much of this is amateur depends on the ITU region: 3.5–3.8 MHz in Region 1, 3.5–4.0 in Region 2, 3.5–3.9 in Region 3.

name: 80/75 m amateur (Region 2)
notes: A full 500 kHz, with the SSB end above 3.8 MHz.

name: Maritime mobile (4 MHz)
notes: 4207.5 kHz is the 4 MHz DSC calling channel.

name: 60 m amateur
notes: The WRC-15 secondary allocation: 15 W EIRP, and a band the amateur service shares with fixed and mobile users who were there first.

name: ISM — 6.78 MHz
notes: RR 5.138: industrial, scientific and medical.

name: 40 m amateur
notes: Lower sideband. 7.2–7.3 MHz is amateur in Region 2 and shortwave broadcast everywhere else, which is why 40 m sounds different depending on where you are.

name: 40 m amateur (Region 2 extension)
notes: Shortwave broadcast to the rest of the world, amateur here.

name: Maritime mobile (8 MHz)
notes: 8414.5 kHz is the 8 MHz DSC calling channel.

name: 30 m amateur
notes: A WARC band: CW and narrow digital only by IARU convention, no contests, and usually a 200 W ceiling.

name: HF aeronautical mobile (off-route)
notes: 11175 kHz is the primary US Air Force HFGCS channel.

name: Radio astronomy — 13.36 MHz
notes: A passive band: no emission is permitted.

name: ISM — 13.56 MHz
notes: RR 5.150. NFC and HF RFID.

name: 20 m amateur
notes: Upper sideband above 10 MHz by convention. The band that is open somewhere almost all the time.

name: 17 m amateur
notes: A WARC band: no contesting by IARU convention, so it stays civil.

name: 15 m amateur
notes: A daytime DX band that follows the solar cycle closely.

name: 12 m amateur
notes: A WARC band, and the quietest of the high bands.

name: CB channels 41–80
notes: Germany licenses 80 CB channels rather than the CEPT 40; 41–80 are FM only.

name: ISM — 27 MHz
notes: RR 5.150. The Citizens' Band channel plans sit inside it, as does a great deal of radio control and industrial heating.

name: Citizens Band — 40 channels
notes: 4 W AM carrier, 12 W PEP SSB. Channel 9 (27.065 MHz) is emergency, channel 19 (27.185 MHz) the highway channel.

name: CB 27/81 — UK FM channels
notes: The UK's own 40-channel FM allocation from 1981, still authorised alongside the CEPT channels below it.

name: 10 m amateur
notes: Dead at solar minimum and worldwide at maximum. 29.6 MHz is the FM calling channel.

name: VHF low-band land mobile
notes: Long-range fleet, utility and forestry radio. Sporadic-E carries it across a continent for weeks at a time in early summer.

name: ISM — 40.68 MHz
notes: RR 5.150. Model control and low-power telemetry.

name: VHF fixed, mobile and broadcast
notes: The old television Band I in Region 1; 50–54 MHz is the 6 m amateur band in Regions 2 and 3, and 50–52 MHz in most of Region 1 since WRC-19.

name: 6 m amateur (Region 1)
notes: WRC-19 harmonised 50–52 MHz across Region 1; some administrations allow up to 54 MHz. Sporadic-E turns it into a worldwide band for hours at a time.

name: OIRT FM broadcast
notes: The legacy Eastern-European FM band; still on air in a few places.

name: 4 m amateur
notes: A Region 1 speciality and the UK has the widest slice of it: 70.450 MHz is the FM calling channel, 70.200 MHz the SSB centre.

name: 4 m amateur
notes: A 30 kHz secondary allocation, CW and SSB only — a sliver next to the UK's 500 kHz on the same band.

name: Marker beacons — 75 MHz
notes: Airport marker beacons, keyed at 400, 1300 or 3000 Hz.

name: BOS 4 m band
notes: Legacy analogue public-safety radio. Largely migrated to BOS-Digitalfunk in 380–400 MHz, but fire brigades still run paging and fallback traffic here.

name: FM broadcast
notes: ±75 kHz deviation, a 19 kHz stereo pilot, and RDS on a 57 kHz subcarrier. Region 2 starts at 88.0 MHz with a 200 kHz raster.

name: UKW broadcast
notes: The public and private FM networks, with RDS on essentially all of them.

name: FM broadcast
notes: The BBC national networks cluster between 88 and 94.6 MHz.

name: VOR and ILS localizer
notes: Each carries a Morse ident you can read straight off the AM audio.

name: Airband — civil aviation voice
notes: AM, so a stronger station does not capture a weaker one. 25 kHz spacing, 8.33 kHz across much of Europe. 121.5 MHz is the emergency frequency and is normally silent.

name: Meteorological satellite downlink
notes: NOAA APT at 137.100, 137.620 and 137.9125 MHz; Meteor-M LRPT nearby. Right-hand circular polarisation, so a linear antenna loses 3 dB.

name: 2 m amateur
notes: 145.500 MHz is the Region 1 FM calling channel and 144.800 MHz carries APRS. Regions 2 and 3 have 2 MHz more, up to 148 MHz.

name: Marine VHF
notes: Channel 16 (156.800 MHz) is distress, safety and calling; channel 70 (156.525 MHz) is DSC data only and carries no voice.

name: AIS — 161.975 and 162.025 MHz
notes: AIS 1 and AIS 2, 9600 baud GMSK in 25 kHz channels. Both are decoded at once if the receiver's span covers them.

name: NOAA Weather Radio
notes: Seven channels of continuous forecast voice, plus SAME alert tones that also drive the emergency alert system.

name: BOS 2 m band
notes: Analogue public-safety VHF, and where POCSAG fire paging still runs.

name: VHF television — channels 7–13
notes: Region 2 uses Band III for television, where Region 1 put DAB — the same spectrum, a completely different sound on a scope.

name: VHF Band III — DAB and television
notes: DAB+ ensembles occupy 1.536 MHz each on the 5A–13F block raster in Region 1; Region 2 uses the band for television channels 7–13.

name: DAB+ — VHF Band III
notes: The national ensemble sits on block 5C (178.352 MHz); the Länder ensembles fill the rest.

name: DAB — VHF Band III
notes: BBC National DAB on block 12B (225.648 MHz), Digital One on 11D, and a dense layer of local multiplexes.

name: UHF military air band
notes: AM like the civil band, running 225–400 MHz in most administrations. 243.0 MHz is the military emergency frequency.

name: ILS glide path
notes: Paired with a localizer in 108–112 MHz; the pairing is fixed by ICAO.

name: BOS-Digitalfunk (TETRA)
notes: The national public-safety TETRA network. Encrypted, so a scope shows the carriers and nothing else.

name: Airwave — emergency services
notes: The national public-safety TETRA network.

name: Meteorological aids — radiosondes
notes: Vaisala RS41 and Graw DFM sondes transmit GFSK here twice a day from every upper-air station in the world.

name: Emergency beacons — 406 MHz
notes: COSPAS-SARSAT distress beacons. Listening is legal everywhere; transmitting anything here is not.

name: 70 cm amateur
notes: Allocated to the amateur service in all three regions; Regions 2 and 3 extend it to 420–450 MHz. Shared with ISM devices in Region 1.

name: ISM — 433 MHz
notes: RR 5.138, Region 1 only. Car keys, tyre-pressure sensors, weather stations, doorbells — and it sits on top of the 70 cm amateur band.

name: Business radio — simple UK and simple light
notes: Ofcom's shared business channels: taxis, security, events and building sites.

name: FRS and GMRS — 462 MHz
notes: Shared channels: FRS is licence-free at 2 W, GMRS needs a licence for the high-power and repeater channels.

name: FRS and GMRS — 467 MHz
notes: The interstitial FRS channels and the GMRS repeater inputs.

name: UHF television (Region 2)
notes: 6 MHz channels, 14–36 after the repack.

name: UHF television
notes: 8 MHz channels in Regions 1 and 3, 6 MHz in Region 2.

name: UHF television — Freeview
notes: DVB-T2, channels 21–48 after the 700 MHz clearance.

name: Land mobile and short-range devices (860–890 MHz)
Wireless microphones — 863–865 MHz
notes: Licence-exempt radio mics and in-ear monitors, 10 mW ERP.

name: GSM 900 uplink
notes: Handset to base station. Where Region 2 has its 915 MHz ISM band.

name: 900 MHz cellular
notes: GSM/LTE in Region 1; Region 2 puts the 902–928 MHz ISM band here instead.

name: ISM — 915 MHz
notes: RR 5.150 in Region 2, and the reason 915 MHz hardware does not work in Europe. Also the 33 cm amateur band.

name: DME and TACAN
notes: Pulse pairs on a 1 MHz raster, paired with a VOR or ILS.

name: ADS-B and Mode S — 1090 MHz
notes: Transponder replies and extended squitter, 1 Mbit/s PPM. Needs the receiver's own samples at 2 Msps or more, so the channel takes IQ rather than a narrow passband.

name: GNSS — L5, E5 and L2
notes: GPS L5 at 1176.45 MHz, Galileo E5, GLONASS L2 around 1246 MHz.

name: 23 cm amateur
notes: Secondary to radionavigation, and increasingly squeezed by Galileo. Narrowband work clusters around 1296 MHz.

name: Radio astronomy — hydrogen line
notes: Neutral hydrogen radiates at 1420.406 MHz. A passive band worldwide: no emission is permitted, which is why it is quiet enough to hear the galaxy in.

name: Mobile satellite downlink — Inmarsat
notes: 1544–1545 MHz is reserved for distress and safety traffic.

name: GNSS — L1 and E1
notes: GPS L1 at 1575.42 MHz, GLONASS L1 around 1602 MHz.

name: DECT
notes: Cordless telephony: ten 1.728 MHz carriers, TDMA.

name: S-band space operation and telemetry
notes: 2200–2290 MHz is the space-research downlink most cubesats use.

name: 13 cm amateur (Region 1)
notes: Secondary, and shared with the 2.4 GHz ISM band above 2400 MHz.

name: ISM — 2.4 GHz
notes: RR 5.150. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee and microwave ovens, and the lower half is also the 13 cm amateur band.

name: Radio astronomy — 2.69 GHz
notes: A passive band: no emission is permitted.

name: S-band radar
notes: Airport surveillance and weather radar.

name: Radio altimeters
notes: Aircraft radio altimeters — the band whose neighbours the 5G C-band rollout argued about.

name: Wi-Fi 5 GHz — upper
notes: Dynamic frequency selection is mandatory: the radar here has priority.

name: ISM — 5.8 GHz
notes: RR 5.150. Also the 6 cm amateur band and where analogue FPV video lives.
